Short conceptual questions to test your grasp of *why* penalized regression exists. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What does "**p ≫ n**" mean for a gene-expression dataset, and why is that shape a problem for ordinary least squares?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Count the predictors versus the samples. What does the model need in order to have a unique solution?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$p$ is the number of predictors (genes) and $n$ is the number of samples (patients/cells); $p \gg n$ means **far more genes than samples**. Each sample is one equation and each coefficient one unknown. With $p > n$ there are more unknowns than equations, so **infinitely many** sets of coefficients fit the data perfectly: there is **no unique** solution — the model is unidentifiable.
:::

---

**Q2.** A study measures 25 patients and fits a linear model with an intercept and 40 genes. How many equations and how many unknowns are there? What will `lm()` report for some of the genes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One equation per patient, one unknown per coefficient (do not forget the intercept).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
25 equations and 41 unknowns (intercept + 40 genes). There are more unknowns than equations, so infinitely many coefficient sets fit perfectly. `lm()` estimates the intercept and 24 genes and returns `NA` for the other **16**, and it fits all 25 patients exactly.
:::

---

**Q3. (optional)** In the matrix form $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}$, why exactly does $p > n$ make $X^\top X$ non-invertible? Use the word **rank**.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The rank of $X^\top X$ cannot exceed the number of samples. When is a $p\times p$ matrix invertible?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\text{rank}(X^\top X) \le n$. A $p \times p$ matrix is invertible only if its rank equals $p$. When $p > n$, the rank is at most $n < p$, so the matrix is **rank-deficient (singular)** and has no inverse.
:::

---

**Q4.** Suppose $p < n$, so there are more samples than coefficients. Name a common biological situation that still makes ordinary least squares coefficients huge and unstable, and say why.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think about genes in the same pathway. Can two genes that always move together be told apart?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correlated predictors** — co-regulated genes move together, so one can stand in for the other. Very different coefficient pairs (say $1, 1$ or $100, -98$) then give almost the same predictions: the data pin down the **sum** of the two coefficients but not the **split**. The noise decides which split ordinary least squares returns, so the coefficients become **large and unstable** (multicollinearity).
:::

---

**Q5.** True or false: the model that fits the training data best is the best model. Explain.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do we actually want the model to do — describe this data, or predict new data?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**False.** A model flexible enough to fit the training data perfectly usually has learned the **noise**, not the signal, and predicts **new** data badly — it **overfits**. We care about generalisation to the next patient, not a perfect fit to the samples we already have.
:::

---

**Q6.** Define **bias** and **variance** in one sentence each, and say which one ordinary least squares with many predictors suffers from.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One comes from a model that is too rigid, the other from a model that is too flexible.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Bias** is error from a model too rigid to capture the true pattern (underfitting). **Variance** is error from a model so flexible it chases noise and changes wildly between samples (overfitting). Ordinary least squares with many predictors is **low bias, high variance** — it overfits.
:::

---

**Q7.** In words, what does adding a penalty term $\lambda\cdot(\text{coefficient size})$ to the least-squares objective do, and what is the role of $\lambda$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The objective now has two competing parts. What does the second part discourage, and what does $\lambda$ set?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It **charges for large coefficients**, so the fit must justify every unit of coefficient it uses; this shrinks coefficients toward zero and stabilises them. $\lambda \ge 0$ sets **how strong** the penalty is — the **bias–variance dial**: $\lambda = 0$ is ordinary least squares (low bias, high variance), large $\lambda$ heavily shrinks (high bias, low variance).
:::

---

**Q8. (optional)** The ridge penalty changes the normal equations to use $X^\top X + \lambda I$ instead of $X^\top X$. Why does this matrix have an inverse even when $p > n$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does adding $\lambda I$ do to the eigenvalues? When is a matrix invertible?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Adding $\lambda I$ lifts **every eigenvalue** of $X^\top X$ by $\lambda$. A matrix is invertible exactly when none of its eigenvalues is zero, so any zero eigenvalue (which is what made the $p > n$ case singular) becomes $\lambda > 0$. Hence $X^\top X + \lambda I$ is **always invertible** for $\lambda > 0$, and there is again a unique solution.
:::

---

**Q9.** Name one bonus a biologist gets from penalization beyond "the model is now computable," and one price paid for it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think about reproducibility of gene signatures and prediction on new patients — and what shrinkage does to the estimates.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Bonus (any one):** more **stable, reproducible** coefficients that don't flip when you swap a few patients; **better prediction** on held-out patients; and with some penalties (lasso), most coefficients go exactly to zero, giving a short **interpretable gene list**. **Price:** shrinkage introduces **bias** — the estimates are systematically pulled toward zero, so choosing $\lambda$ well (later, by cross-validation) matters.
:::
